conclusion.justification: The report finds evidence supporting the idea that opening a window to improve bedroom ventilation and lower CO2 levels can enhance sleep quality, but cautions that the claim is context-dependent and not a universal rule (e.g., opening internal doors lowers CO2 without reliably improving sleep, and open windows can introduce noise or pollution). Therefore, it leans towards endorsing the claim with caveats.

report:
Your skepticism is partly justified: the claim is **overstated as a universal rule**, but not simply false. Reviews say bedroom-air evidence is still limited, yet poor ventilation/high CO₂ is associated with worse sleep and next-day performance (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132320306004). A 40-bedroom Danish field intervention found opening a **window** improved IAQ and objective/subjective sleep, while opening an internal **door** lowered CO₂ but did **not** improve sleep (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605). Other work suggests lower CO₂ is better: ~750 ppm outperformed ~1000–1300 ppm, implying “some ventilation” may still be suboptimal (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459). Controlled chamber data also link very high CO₂ (1900–3000 ppm) with disturbed sleep (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32979003/).

Practical conclusion: improving bedroom ventilation/CO₂ can help, but “open a window or door” is context-dependent. Open windows may backfire with noise, cold/heat, pollen, pollution, or security concerns; doors may reduce CO₂ without reliably improving sleep. The strongest supported version is: keep bedroom air fresh—ideally CO₂ roughly below ~750–1000 ppm—while preserving quiet, darkness, and comfortable temperature.
